To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
green tea and its polyphenolic components possess potent cancer chemoprevention and possible therapeutic potential against human CaP.
GTP and black tea polyphenols are effective in inhibiting growth and progression of human prostate cancer in nude mice and their effects appear to be mediated through induction of apoptosis.
GTP, water extract of black teas, epigallocatechin gallate and theafluavins, respectively inhibit growth of human prostate tumors in athymic mice.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the chemopreventative effects of GTP and its major constituents on CaP.
the identification of novel CaP chemoprotective agents, which could be developed into dietary supplements or chemopreventives.
identifying the chemopreventative potential of tea polyphenols in a pre-clinical CaP model.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
all tea ingredients tested in this study possess chemopreventative and possibly therapeutic effects in CaP.
all the tea ingredients, including GTP, are effective in reducing tumor growth, and in inhibiting PSA secretion and VEGF expression in the CWR22Rnual model.

all the tested tea ingredients possess CaP cancer preventive and therapeutic effects in vivo, which are mediated, at least in part, through induction of apoptosis and inhibition of tumor angiogenesis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
GTP and theaflavin, the major polyphenols present both in green and black teas, respectively, have similar chemopreventative effects in CWR22Rnui1 tumor model in athymic mice.
GTP, as a whole or as a combination of its major constituents epigallocathecin-3-gallates and theaflavin, possess CaP chemoprereventive and therapeutic effects in vivo.

GTP, as well as black tea extract, and their major components epigallocatechin 3-gallate or theaflavines, respectively, are promising chemoprevention agents for human CaP, with GTP having additional therapeutic effects.
The main takeaway from our work is that
GTP and theaflavin (TF), the major constituents of green and black tea, respectively, have similar CaP cancer chemoprreventive effects.
GTP, black tea extract and their major constituents have CaP chemoprotective effects in vivo, and that GTP is a promising candidate for chemopreventation and possibly treatment of CaP in humans.
